what: Realty Income owns over 15,500 freestanding properties leased to businesses in the United States, the United Kingdom and Europe. Tenants pay rent plus taxes, insurance and maintenance, and it pays its shareholders monthly.
customers: Retail chains, convenience stores, dollar stores, grocers, gyms, cinemas and industrial tenants on long leases.
money: long-term net leases, mostly to retail tenants
moat: Scale and a low cost of capital that lets it buy large property portfolios others cannot finance, spread across thousands of tenants so no single failure matters.
risks: Debt of about $27 billion makes it very sensitive to interest rates
Growth depends on issuing shares to fund acquisitions, which dilutes holders when the share price is low
Some tenants, such as cinemas and pharmacies, are in declining industries
Return on invested capital is low by design, as with all landlords
opportunities: A dividend yield near 5.6%, paid monthly and raised for three decades
Leases typically run over a decade with built-in rent increases
European expansion opens a market with less competition for net-lease deals
watch: Occupancy, the acquisition cap rate against its cost of capital, and AFFO per share.
